title: The One With The Halloween Party

jokes.text: Tell me you're not gonna dress like a dinosaur. / Not two years in a row.
jokes.setup: Ross says he has to wear a costume to his classes anyway
jokes.punchline: The implication that he wore a dinosaur costume to teach last year — and his response only denies a second consecutive year, implying he absolutely did it once
jokes.explanation: Beautifully economical. The punchline doesn't deny wearing the dinosaur costume — it only denies wearing it two years in a row. That implication gap is where the comedy lives. Tight structure, strong character integration (Ross's paleontology obsession), and the audience fills in the rest. One of the stronger early jokes.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: We're having a Halloween party! Costumes are mandatory.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: No.

jokes.text: Halloween is stupid. Dressing up, pretending to be someone you're not. / You're an actor.
jokes.setup: Chandler refuses to dress up, philosophizing that pretending to be someone you're not is stupid
jokes.punchline: Joey (an actor) immediately undercuts the logic by pointing out Chandler is talking to a professional pretender
jokes.explanation: Three words demolish Chandler's entire argument. Perfect economy — Joey doesn't elaborate, he doesn't need to. The irony is sharp and the character integration is strong since it's Joey specifically who would think of this.

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: I wore the dinosaur costume to teach in!

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: Ross, that's the most inappropriate thing you could wear to a classroom.

jokes.text: If she needs costume ideas, she could be a bikini model, or a slutty nurse, or a sexy cheerleader. Or Leatherface from Texas Chainsaw Massacre. No! Slutty Leatherface.
jokes.setup: Joey is suggesting sexy costume ideas for Mona
jokes.punchline: The list escalates from sexy to horrific (Leatherface), then Joey immediately reframes the horror character as 'slutty' — his one-track mind overriding even a chainsaw murderer
jokes.explanation: The escalation from conventionally sexy to Leatherface is an unexpected swerve, and then 'Slutty Leatherface' snaps it back to Joey's singular obsession. The self-correction is the best part — it's pure Joey logic applied relentlessly. Strong character integration.

dialogue.speaker: Unknown
dialogue.line: Halloween is just pretending to be someone you're not.

dialogue.speaker: Unknown
dialogue.line: Yeah, well you're an actor.

jokes.text: And I got her. I guess the better man won. / Please don't take her from me.
jokes.setup: Ross gloats that he beat Joey for Mona's attention
jokes.punchline: Joey's immediate, sincere-sounding plea undercuts Ross's triumphalism and reveals Joey's genuinely sad romantic scorekeeping
jokes.explanation: Joey's sincere desperation is funny but leans on a familiar beat. The juxtaposition works, but it's not especially original in the Friends universe.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: You could go as a scary movie villain. Like a slutty Jason.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: Or a slutty Freddy Krueger.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: Ooh! Slutty Michael Myers!

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: You know what? Slutty Hannibal Lecter. You'd wear a ball gag... but like, in a sexy way.

jokes.text: Ursula! / Wait. It's me, Phoebe. I thought there was a mirror there.
jokes.setup: Phoebe calls out to someone she thinks is Ursula
jokes.punchline: It IS Ursula, but Phoebe explains she mistook her for her own reflection — meaning Phoebe thought she was looking at herself, which reveals they're dressed identically
jokes.explanation: The twin-mistaken-for-mirror gag is a visual comedy staple but it's executed well here. The payoff requires the audience to realize both what happened and what it implies about their appearance. Solid visual comedy that plays better on screen.

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: Yeah, well, I won Mona fair and square.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: Did you?

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: Yes! She chose me over you.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: Okay...

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: She did! Right? She chose me? She's still choosing me? Tell me she's still choosing me!

jokes.text: It'll be a small ceremony. Just family. / His.
jokes.setup: Ursula says the wedding will just be family
jokes.punchline: One-word clarification: only his family — implying the sisters' relationship is so bad that Phoebe isn't considered family by Ursula
jokes.explanation: One word. 'His.' The ruthless economy of this joke is exceptional — Ursula casually excludes her own twin sister from her wedding with a single syllable. The dark undercurrent of their dysfunctional relationship adds weight. Strong structure: setup builds warmth, punchline devastates with minimum syllables.

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: Ursula!

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: Oh my God, I thought you were my reflection.

jokes.text: If you want to come, I guess that'd be okay. You could be my sister for the day.
jokes.setup: Ursula grudgingly invites Phoebe to the wedding
jokes.punchline: She says Phoebe could 'be her sister for the day' — Phoebe IS her sister, making this a casually devastating dismissal of their actual relationship
jokes.explanation: A dark comedic beat — Ursula is so casually cruel she doesn't even acknowledge the absurdity of what she's said. Builds on joke #7's tone effectively.

dialogue.speaker: Ursula
dialogue.line: We're having a small ceremony with just family.

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: What do you mean 'just family'? I'm family!

dialogue.speaker: Ursula
dialogue.line: His family. Not mine.

jokes.text: It's a costume party. / So that's why you're.. / No. / But thanks.
jokes.setup: Phoebe mentions it's a costume party, and Ursula starts to comment on Phoebe's appearance
jokes.punchline: Ursula implies Phoebe is already dressed strangely enough to look like a costume. Phoebe's 'No. But thanks.' accepts the insult with resigned dignity.
jokes.explanation: The incomplete sentence from Ursula and Phoebe's resigned 'But thanks' does a lot of work. Economical and character-appropriate — Phoebe is used to this treatment from Ursula.

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: No, these are my regular clothes.

jokes.text: I am a woman who spent money on a dress she wants to wear because soon she won't fit into it.
jokes.setup: Rachel is asked what her costume is at the Halloween party
jokes.punchline: Her 'costume' is just a dress she wants to wear before her pregnancy makes it impossible — she's weaponized the costume party as an excuse to wear something she loves
jokes.explanation: Sweet and character-revealing — Rachel's vanity and practicality merging into one move. Not a big laugh but a warm, relatable character moment that gets a knowing chuckle.

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: I'm not wearing a costume. I'm pregnant.

jokes.text: I'm Catwoman, who wants the dress when you're too big for it.
jokes.setup: Rachel has established her 'costume' is about wearing the dress before pregnancy
jokes.punchline: She's already scheming to pass the dress on — mid-sentence pivoting from character introduction to wardrobe logistics
jokes.explanation: A quick button on the previous joke. The mid-sentence topic switch from Catwoman to dress-redistribution is funny but mild. Works as a tag.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: Wait, wait, wait. So when you're done with it, you're gonna give it to me, right?

jokes.text: I want to be with kids. Since I got pregnant, I have maternal instincts.
jokes.setup: Rachel asks to give out candy to trick-or-treaters
jokes.punchline: Rachel claiming maternal instincts as a pregnant woman wanting to distribute Halloween candy — the mundane context undercuts the grandeur of 'maternal instincts'
jokes.explanation: Mildly amusing setup for a later payoff. The joke itself is thin — 'maternal instincts = giving out candy' is not a sharp enough observation on its own.

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: Well, see, the thing about fashion is that it's not just about clothes, it's about expressing yourself and—

dialogue.speaker: Kid
dialogue.line: Can I have some candy?

jokes.text: And you are so in style right now. / I work at Ralph Lauren. The fall line has got this equestrian theme. / Did you see the cover of Vogue..? / Could I just have the candy?
jokes.setup: Rachel gives out candy to trick-or-treaters and compliments a child's horse costume
jokes.punchline: Rachel launches into a fashion lecture about Ralph Lauren's equestrian theme to a small child who just wants candy
jokes.explanation: Perfect character comedy. Rachel cannot suppress her fashion instincts even when talking to a trick-or-treater. The child's deadpan 'Could I just have the candy?' is the ideal straight-man response. This is exactly what Rachel would do and the audience recognizes it immediately.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: I have never worn a bunny costume in my life. Well, except for that Easter in 1987, but we agreed never to speak of that again.

jokes.text: Catwoman. So we meet again. / So we do, Supergirl. / It's me, Phoebe.
jokes.setup: Rachel (Catwoman) greets Monica (Supergirl) with mock-villain drama
jokes.punchline: Monica plays along, but Phoebe is behind Monica and thinks she's being spoken to — breaking the theatrical moment with mundane clarification
jokes.explanation: A brief, mild comedic misunderstanding. Functions as a quick beat but doesn't have a strong payoff.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: What do you mean 'dressed up'? I'm not dressed up.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: I'm dressed as Chandler.

jokes.text: He loves The Velveteen Rabbit. / That rabbit was brown and white. / It was pink, or no bunny at all. / No bunny at all. Always no bunny at all!
jokes.setup: Monica has dressed Chandler as a pink bunny, claiming he loves The Velveteen Rabbit
jokes.punchline: Their exchange reveals Monica's controlling nature — she gave him an ultimatum of pink bunny or no bunny at all, and Chandler's anguished 'Always no bunny at all!' shows he would have preferred neither
jokes.explanation: Classic Monica/Chandler dynamic — her controlling perfectionism, his defeated compliance. 'No bunny at all. Always no bunny at all!' is a great escalating callback within the same joke. The pink correction is very Monica: she didn't just dress him up, she dressed him up WRONG. Strong character integration for both.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: I do not sound like that.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: I do not sound like that.

jokes.text: You didn't dress up either? / Yes, I did. I'm Chandler.
jokes.setup: Ross hasn't dressed up; Joey asks him why
jokes.punchline: Joey reveals his 'costume' is Chandler — implying that whatever he's doing physically is a spot-on impression of Chandler
jokes.explanation: The setup (Ross not dressing up) is a misdirect — the real joke is Joey's costume. 'I'm Chandler' lands as a great reveal because we see whatever physical bit Joey is doing. The fact that it's apparently recognizable is the deeper joke about Chandler's mannerisms. Strong economy and character integration.

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: Oh my God, look at you! You're so cute! Okay, new rule: you can only eat the candy if you say 'please' in baby talk. Can you do that? Say 'peeeease'?

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: And another rule—you have to hop on one foot to the next house. It's much more fun that way!

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: Oh! And you can't have any chocolate, only gummies. Actually, wait—no gummies either. Just the red candies. The red ones are the best for you.

jokes.text: How is that me? / I'm Chandler. / That is so you! / When have I ever done that? / When have I ever done that?
jokes.setup: Chandler protests that Joey's impression of him is inaccurate
jokes.punchline: Chandler asks 'When have I ever done that?' while unconsciously mimicking the exact mannerism Joey is performing — Ross confirms it
jokes.explanation: The repeated 'When have I ever done that?' while DOING THE THING is a beautifully constructed piece of physical comedy. The irony is ironclad — Chandler denies the mannerism while performing it in real time. This is elevated by being entirely dependent on a visual we can only infer from dialogue, making it stronger on rewatches. Among the episode's best.

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: I gave away all my candy because she said she loved me!

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: Rachel, you're pregnant.

jokes.text: You're the prettiest ballerina ever. / Thank you. / That deserves another candy. / Thank you. / I have to say, that earns 'two-two' pieces of candy. / I love you! / Honey, here, take it all.
jokes.setup: A little ballerina trick-or-treater arrives; Rachel earlier claimed maternal instincts
jokes.punchline: Rachel's 'maternal instincts' manifest as hopelessly spoiling a child with increasingly more candy until she gives her everything — undercutting her earlier claim with absurd reality
jokes.explanation: The escalation is well-paced — candy, more candy, 'two-two,' 'I love you,' everything. It's a callback to Rachel's maternal instincts claim that reveals she's completely unprepared for actual children. The 'two-two' wordplay is a cute touch. 'Take it all' is a satisfying button.

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: It's a potato… that's also Sputnik. Get it? Because Sputnik is Russian, and Russians eat a lot of potatoes.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: Yeah, we got it.

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: So it's a Sput-nik... a Spud-nik!

jokes.text: But one said she loved me, so I gave her everything.
jokes.setup: Monica asks why there's no candy left after only four kids.
jokes.punchline: Rachel's matter-of-fact confession that she gave everything away because one child said 'I love you.'
jokes.explanation: Clean callback with great economy. Rachel's deadpan delivery of this absurd reasoning — framed as perfectly logical — is the culmination of the candy bit and works as a satisfying button.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: Hey, that's not a potato. That's a butt.

jokes.text: No wonder you're pregnant.
jokes.setup: Rachel has given all the candy away because one child said she loved her
jokes.punchline: Monica's one-liner implies Rachel is so easily won over that it's no surprise she got pregnant
jokes.explanation: Sharp, mean-spirited (in the best Friends tradition), and economical. The logical leap from 'gives everything to anyone who says I love you' to 'that's how she got pregnant' is fast and funny. High quotability — it's the kind of line people repeat.

dialogue.speaker: Eric
dialogue.line: Wait, you're Phoebe? Not Ursula?

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: Yeah, I'm Phoebe. Why?

dialogue.speaker: Eric
dialogue.line: Oh my God. Oh my God, no...

jokes.text: Remember the satellite, Sputnik? Well, I'm a potato. Or a 'spud'.. and these are my antenna. So Sputnik becomes..? Spud-nik!
jokes.setup: Someone asks Ross what his costume is supposed to be
jokes.punchline: Ross has dressed as a potato with antennae to make the pun 'Spud-nik' — an obscure science pun that required significant costume effort
jokes.explanation: This is quintessential Ross — an elaborate science pun costume that required real effort and that nobody will appreciate. The costume design exists entirely to serve a wordplay joke only a scientist-nerd would make. Perfect character integration: only Ross would do this. The reveal lands well, and the buildup ('so Sputnik becomes..?') adds comedic anticipation.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: Why did you slap her?

dialogue.speaker: Eric
dialogue.line: I thought she was someone else!

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: So what, now you're just slapping random people?

dialogue.speaker: Eric
dialogue.line: Well, maybe if we all slapped each other, nobody would feel singled out.

jokes.text: Wow! I don't have the worst costume anymore.
jokes.setup: Chandler has been suffering in his pink bunny costume
jokes.punchline: Ross's Spud-nik costume is so bad it makes Chandler's bunny look better by comparison
jokes.explanation: A quick, satisfying callback. Chandler's relief is relatable and the line is delivered with perfect deadpan. Brief but effective.

dialogue.speaker: Eric
dialogue.line: Maybe you should try to contact your mother. You know, do a séance or something.

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: My mother killed herself.

dialogue.speaker: Eric
dialogue.line: Oh. Well, that would make the séance a lot easier then.

jokes.text: All right! Ross came as doodie.
jokes.setup: Ross appears in his Spud-nik costume
jokes.punchline: The antennae and brown potato costume reads to everyone else as a piece of poop
jokes.explanation: The 'doodie' misread is funny but not especially clever — poop jokes are a low bar. It earns its laugh from the contrast with Ross's intellectual intention. Functions well as a crowd reaction.

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: I love second grade.

dialogue.speaker: Eric
dialogue.line: Second grade? That's middle management. You gotta work your way up from kindergarten.

jokes.text: No, I'm not doodie. / No, space-doodie.
jokes.setup: Ross protests that he's not doodie
jokes.punchline: Joey's correction — 'space-doodie' — doesn't defend Ross at all, just recontextualizes the poop in space
jokes.explanation: 'Space-doodie' is a great small joke — Joey thinks he's being helpful by being more precise, but precision here just makes the insult more elaborate. Perfect Joey logic.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: Who would win a fight between Catwoman and Supergirl?

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: I don't know, but I know Phoebe would beat them both.

jokes.text: Aren't you gonna kiss me? / Okay. But right after, you have to tell me who you are.
jokes.setup: Eric (Ursula's fiancé) kisses someone he thinks is Ursula at the party
jokes.punchline: He doesn't know it's Phoebe — his request to 'tell me who you are' after kissing reveals the mistaken identity
jokes.explanation: A classic mistaken-identity beat. Works well as a plot setup but the joke itself is functional rather than exceptional.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: Phoebe would win any fight. She's lived on the streets, she's been in and out of jail, she sold her body for... other things.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: Joey!

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: What? I'm just saying, the woman is tough!

jokes.text: You're the sister. I just slapped my future sister-in-law's ass.
jokes.setup: Eric realizes he's been with Phoebe, not Ursula
jokes.punchline: His mortification is expressed through the specific horror of having slapped his future sister-in-law's butt
jokes.explanation: The specific nature of his transgression (not just 'I touched you' but 'I slapped your ass') elevates this from generic embarrassment to specific cringe. Well-delivered.

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: As if! I mean, please. Ross can barely open a jar, and Chandler? He runs like a girl.

jokes.text: Is your mother here? I could slap her on the butt. / My mother killed herself. / See, and I knew that.
jokes.setup: Eric tries to defuse his accidental ass-slap with self-deprecating humor
jokes.punchline: His joke about slapping the mother lands horribly — she's dead by suicide. Eric's 'See, and I knew that' shows he knew it and said it anyway, compounding the disaster
jokes.explanation: 'See, and I knew that' is a great dark comedy line. Eric has dug himself so deep that he's moved past recovery into pure mortification. The joke weaponizes his own awareness — he KNEW her mother was dead and his brain still offered the joke. The self-awareness makes it funnier and more cringe-worthy. Strong dark comedy moment.

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: He's so hot, even when he's all sweaty. I'd totally mop him up.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: That's gross.

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: What? I meant like in basketball!

jokes.text: Now I'm sweating. I'm sweating. Now I'm saying look at me, I'm even sweatier. I should go.
jokes.setup: Eric has just made several awful social blunders in quick succession
jokes.punchline: His self-conscious commentary on his own sweating makes the sweating worse, which he notices, creating an anxiety spiral he narrates in real time
jokes.explanation: Nicely observed social anxiety comedy. The self-referential loop of noticing the sweat, mentioning it, and making it worse by mentioning it is a recognizable human experience made funny through escalation.

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: I know you are but what am I?

jokes.text: What are you? / There's no name for it. I get nervous, and I sweat like crazy. / No, I meant your costume.
jokes.setup: Phoebe asks Eric what he is (meaning his costume)
jokes.punchline: Eric interprets it as a question about his sweating condition — a perfect deflation when Phoebe clarifies she meant his costume
jokes.explanation: The misdirection works because Eric is so deep in his anxiety spiral that his brain immediately goes to the sweat as the defining thing about him. 'There's no name for it' as a descriptor of his sweating condition is a solid punchline within the punchline.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: What's your name?

dialogue.speaker: Kid
dialogue.line: Jkhxcvbnmsdhfkuerbvnmxcvbsdhfbvxcvbsdhfbvxcvbsdhfbvxcvbsdhfbvxcvb

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: How about we just call you 'Bob'?

jokes.text: I love the second grade. / Really? / It's much better than first grade, and definitely better than third. With all the politics and the mind games.
jokes.setup: Eric mentions his second-grade students helped with his costume
jokes.punchline: Phoebe enthusiastically endorses second grade over other grades, then characterizes third grade as a hotbed of 'politics and mind games' — attributing adult social complexity to 8-year-olds
jokes.explanation: Quintessential Phoebe comedy — she speaks with absolute conviction about something completely absurd. 'The politics and mind games of third grade' is a great line because Phoebe treats it as self-evident truth. Strong character integration; this is Phoebe's comedic voice perfectly deployed.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: Why don't you wear that sexy nurse costume I suggested?

dialogue.speaker: Mona
dialogue.line: I'm an actual nurse, Joey.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: Exactly! So you're already halfway there!

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: Joey, that's not helpful.

jokes.text: She's the most beautiful woman ever. / Thank you.
jokes.setup: Eric talks about Ursula with Phoebe, unaware Phoebe is her twin sister
jokes.punchline: Phoebe instinctively says 'thank you' to a compliment about Ursula's looks, because she's being complimented about her own appearance by extension
jokes.explanation: A quick, well-timed reaction beat. Phoebe's 'thank you' is perfectly ambiguous — she knows she's the same face, so she accepts the compliment. Economical and sweet.

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: I mean, what's wrong with a sexy nurse? Nurses are sexy.

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: Ross!

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: What? I'm just saying, they have those little caps, and the shoes...

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: Oh my God, Ross, stop talking.

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: You know what? I don't even care anymore. I've said so much weird stuff in front of you people, nothing could embarrass me now.

jokes.text: Who would win in a fight, Catwoman or Supergirl? / Catwoman, hands down. / Between you and Phoebe? I'd give Phoebe the edge. / She's not right behind me, is she?
jokes.setup: Joey is asked who would win between Catwoman and Supergirl as a hypothetical
jokes.punchline: Joey immediately applies the question to the real people wearing the costumes, decides Phoebe would beat Rachel, then panics about whether Phoebe heard
jokes.explanation: Joey's reasoning — 'Phoebe lived on the street' — is funny because it's both absurd and oddly logical. His immediate self-preservation instinct ('She's not right behind me, is she?') is very Joey.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: Hey, if she laughs at your jokes, marry her!

jokes.text: Phoebe lived on the street, okay? Plus, she's got a crazy temper.
jokes.setup: Joey explains why Phoebe would beat Rachel in a fight
jokes.punchline: Joey's reasoning is oddly specific and accurate — Phoebe's backstory as a homeless youth is treated as a legit fighting credential
jokes.explanation: Joey treats Phoebe's tragic homeless past as a street-fighting credential — it's funny because it's accurate within the show's mythology. Good character work for both Phoebe and Joey.

dialogue.speaker: Ursula
dialogue.line: I founded a town in the Peace Corps. It's called Ursulapolis.

jokes.text: What if I told you Ross or Chandler could beat you up? / I would say, 'Woman, please.'
jokes.setup: Rachel pushes back on Joey's fight assessment
jokes.punchline: 'Woman, please' — Joey's dismissal is so confident and specific it becomes funny. The phrase itself carries comedic weight.
jokes.explanation: 'Woman, please' is a quotable, economical dismissal. Joey's confidence in his physical superiority over Ross and Chandler is well-founded and funny. High quotability.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: I could make jokes about my humiliating costume, but I'd just be trying too hard. Which, let's face it, is my signature move.

jokes.text: You think you could take him? / The dude with the balls on his chest? I think so.
jokes.setup: Monica asks if Phoebe could beat Eric (the solar system guy) in a fight
jokes.punchline: Phoebe's reference to 'the dude with the balls on his chest' reduces Eric's cosmic costume to a crude anatomical description
jokes.explanation: The inadvertent double entendre ('balls on his chest' = planet spheres) gets a mild laugh. Quick and functional.

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: I'm telling you, I could take you in a fight.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: Oh please, you'd cry.

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: I would not cry!

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: You cried at that commercial with the kitten.

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: That was... that was different.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: How about we arm wrestle then, tough guy?

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: You're on!

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: Okay, one... two...

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: Ow! Ow! Uncle! Uncle!

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: That's what I thought.

jokes.text: Oh, my God, Phoebe? You're getting a crush on him. / No, I'm not, you are! / Here comes the temper.
jokes.setup: Phoebe has been enthusiastically describing Eric's virtues
jokes.punchline: Monica calls out the crush; Phoebe's childish 'No, I'm not, you are!' denial, followed immediately by Monica's knowing 'Here comes the temper' — confirming Joey's earlier assessment
jokes.explanation: 'Here comes the temper' is a great callback to Joey's earlier assessment. Phoebe's response ('No, I'm not, you are!') is perfectly childish for the character and immediately proves Monica's point. The callback gives it extra punch.

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: You're going down.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: Oh yeah? Well, you're going... down. Harder.

jokes.text: And I've been giving out money, but I'm out of that too. / Can I write you a check? / Okay. What's your name? / Lelani Mayolanofavich. / Okay, I'm just gonna write this out to 'cash.'
jokes.setup: Monica has run out of candy and money for trick-or-treaters
jokes.punchline: She offers a check to a child, starts to fill it out, gets an impossible surname, and immediately pivots to 'cash' — Monica's OCD problem-solving applied to an absurd situation
jokes.explanation: Monica writing a check to a trick-or-treating child is funny on its own, but the unpronounceable surname forcing the pivot to 'cash' is a perfect payoff. The name itself is a good joke — clearly invented to be unwritable. Monica's pragmatic acceptance is very in-character.

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: Yeah, that's right. We're not guys you want to mess with.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: We're very dangerous.

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: Extremely dangerous.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: You guys are about as intimidating as a couple of kittens in sweaters.

jokes.text: Joey's gonna be thrilled. He was hoping you'd be a slutty nurse. / Actually, I'm just a nurse.
jokes.setup: Ross greets Mona at the party and references Joey's earlier costume suggestion
jokes.punchline: Mona is literally dressed as a plain nurse — Joey's wish was accidentally half-granted but without the 'slutty' qualifier, which deflates the fantasy
jokes.explanation: The callback to Joey's earlier 'slutty nurse' suggestion pays off beautifully — the universe delivered a nurse, just not the right kind. 'Actually, I'm just a nurse' is a perfect deadpan deflation. The gap between Joey's fantasy and reality is the joke.

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: Gunther, you're so sweet for bringing me candy. You're like the nicest guy I know. You're like my best friend.

jokes.text: You'd think that would embarrass me, but I'm maxed out.
jokes.setup: Ross said something awkward about Joey wanting Mona to be a slutty nurse
jokes.punchline: 'I'm maxed out' on embarrassment — Ross has experienced enough humiliation that this doesn't even register
jokes.explanation: 'I'm maxed out' is a genuinely good line — it implies Ross has such a rich history of embarrassment that his humiliation meter is full. Character-specific and economical. Good self-aware Ross moment.

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: You know what? Here comes a really good one.

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: You're... you're a big stupid head!

jokes.text: You're a potato? / Well, I'm a spud.. And the antenna.. You're Spud-nik! / Yes! / Marry her.
jokes.setup: Mona encounters Ross's costume for the first time
jokes.punchline: She gets the Spud-nik pun immediately without needing a lengthy explanation — and Joey's instant 'Marry her' reflects that this is Ross's ideal woman
jokes.explanation: 'Marry her' is a perfect button — two words that do enormous comedic and character work. The earlier scene spent time with no one understanding the costume; Mona gets it instantly. Joey's response encapsulates exactly what Ross needs. This is the payoff to a running gag with excellent economy. One of the episode's best single lines.

dialogue.speaker: Ursula
dialogue.line: It's just a marriage. It's not like it means anything. I mean, I'm probably going to cheat on him anyway.

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: Well, at least call it what it is — an affair, not a 'thing on the side.'

jokes.text: Who'd win a fight between Ross and Chandler? / I can't answer that. Chandler's my husband. / So Ross? / Yeah.
jokes.setup: The fight question is extended to Ross vs. Chandler
jokes.punchline: Monica dodges the question on spousal loyalty grounds — but her confirmation of Ross when pushed makes it obvious she thinks Chandler would lose
jokes.explanation: Monica's reluctant confirmation of Ross is a funny dig at Chandler. Her loyalty conflict is played well — she tries to stay neutral but can't lie. Part of a good running thread through the episode.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: Oh my God, that's the same face you make when we're—

jokes.text: We're both teachers. / And we were both in the Peace Corps. / When we were building in Uruguay, we were two towns apart and never met. / Yeah. It wasn't a town when I got there, but it was a town when I left.
jokes.setup: Eric and Ursula bond over their apparent shared experiences — both teachers, both Peace Corps volunteers
jokes.punchline: Ursula's Peace Corps detail ('it wasn't a town when I got there, but it was a town when I left') sounds like an inspiring backstory but becomes suspicious given everything we know about Ursula
jokes.explanation: The joke is in the dramatic irony — we know Ursula is lying, so her increasingly elaborate backstory becomes funnier. The 'town when I left' line is a good detail that sounds impressive but will later be exposed as fabrication.

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: Well, I've been divorced twice, I'm still in love with Rachel, and I named my son after the woman I was in love with before that. So yeah, I'm definitely the guy to take relationship advice from.

jokes.text: Howdy, doodie. / That's funny, yeah. / You're the funniest man here in a bunny costume his wife made him wear.
jokes.setup: Ross greets Chandler with 'Howdy, Doodie' — a pun on Howdy Doody and the 'doodie' nickname
jokes.punchline: Chandler sardonically acknowledges the joke then immediately cuts Ross down — pointing out that Ross's 'funniest man here' status doesn't mean much given his own humiliating costume situation
jokes.explanation: Chandler's comeback is tidy — he accepts the pun's humor but immediately contextualizes his own degradation. 'In a bunny costume his wife made him wear' is a solid self-deprecating callback.

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: Okay, fine. Fine! Joey was right. The costume was ridiculous.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: Thank you! I've been saying this the whole time!

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: But it was a perfectly accurate historical recreation!

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: No one cares, man. You looked like a freak.

jokes.text: I'll prove it like a theorem!
jokes.setup: Ross and Chandler are about to prove who's stronger
jokes.punchline: Ross invokes mathematical proof language in a physical altercation context — only Ross would issue a trash-talk challenge framed as academic methodology
jokes.explanation: Five words, perfectly in character. 'I'll prove it like a theorem' is Ross's intellectual identity colliding with physical competition in the most specific, funny way possible. It's absurd, quotable, and absolutely character-specific. Only Ross says this. Among the strongest lines of the episode.

jokes.text: You guys could arm-wrestle. / Listen to the slutty nurse.
jokes.setup: Mona (the plain nurse) suggests arm-wrestling to settle the fight
jokes.punchline: Chandler dismisses her with 'slutty nurse' — the costume label Joey wanted applied to the wrong person in the wrong context
jokes.explanation: A callback to the 'slutty nurse' thread — now Chandler uses it dismissively, which is both a character moment (Chandler stress-trash-talking) and a callback payoff.

dialogue.speaker: Ursula
dialogue.line: I need to pray. I need to find my spiritual center.

jokes.text: You're going down. / Oh, yeah? You're going downtown!
jokes.setup: Ross and Chandler trash-talk before the arm-wrestle
jokes.punchline: Chandler's 'You're going downtown' is a botched version of 'going down' — either accidental or intentionally absurd trash-talk
jokes.explanation: 'Going downtown' as a trash-talk response is perfectly bad — it sounds like Chandler panicked and grabbed the wrong phrase. Very Chandler to fumble the trash-talk.

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: So I gave him money to stop crying.

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: Then I had to pretend to be his girlfriend at, like, five different houses.

jokes.text: Seriously, guys, the trash talk is embarrassing.
jokes.setup: Ross and Chandler have been delivering terrible trash talk
jokes.punchline: Mona's dry observation that it's 'embarrassing' validates what the audience already felt — a straight-man punctuation
jokes.explanation: A functional audience surrogate line. Gets a laugh by confirming what everyone's thinking. Not exceptional but well-placed.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: Kids are only bad on Halloween, Rachel. That's it. Just that one day.

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: Really?

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: Well, okay, and Christmas. Kids go crazy on Christmas.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: And their birthdays. Obviously birthdays.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: And the summer. Kids are terrible all summer.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: And during school when they get home. That's bad.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: And spring break.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: And Thanksgiving. Oh God, Thanksgiving is the worst.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: And rainy days when they can't go outside.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: And sunny days when they have too much energy.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: Basically... kids are only good when they're asleep.

jokes.text: Gunther, you brought candy. Thank you so much. You are so sweet. You are gonna make some man the luckiest guy in the world.
jokes.setup: Gunther brings candy and Monica thanks him effusively
jokes.punchline: 'You are gonna make some man the luckiest guy in the world' — Monica accidentally implies Gunther is gay (or at minimum doesn't think he'll attract a woman), which is a dig at his eternal unrequited love for Rachel
jokes.explanation: The joke cuts Gunther at multiple levels — Monica doesn't know she's being insulting (or does she?), and the audience knows his hopeless Rachel obsession makes the 'some man' misdirection particularly funny. Character-rich.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: Kids are difficult when they're teething, when they're potty training, when they're going through puberty, when they're teenagers...

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: Monica, I'm never having kids.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: Oh, you say that now.

jokes.text: My friend Lewis told me you were giving out money. / We were, but now we've got candy. / I'd rather have the money. / That's not your choice. Happy Halloween!
jokes.setup: A trick-or-treater has heard about the money giveaway from his friend
jokes.punchline: The child demands money instead of candy; Monica shuts him down with 'That's not your choice. Happy Halloween!' — Monica's controlling nature applied to Halloween child management
jokes.explanation: Monica's abrupt 'That's not your choice. Happy Halloween!' is very Monica — the forced cheerfulness after shutting down a child is funny. The child's brazenness ('I'd rather have the money') is a good setup for her control-freak response.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: I'm telling you, I'm stronger than I look. I could totally take Monica in an arm wrestle.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: Oh really? You want to do this?

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: Yeah, bring it on!

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: Okay...

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: Oh my God! Ow ow ow ow! Make it stop! I think you broke my arm! I can't feel my fingers! This is it, this is how I go out — defeated by a woman half my size!

jokes.text: Is it fair that you put on a cape and get stuff? / Shut up! / You shut up! / You can't tell me to shut up. / I think I just did. And here it comes again. Shut up!
jokes.setup: A trick-or-treater complains that the candy arrangement isn't fair
jokes.punchline: Monica and a small child devolve into a 'shut up' argument, with Monica fully engaging at the child's level
jokes.explanation: Monica arguing with a child at the child's level is perfect character comedy. Her 'I think I just did' is a great escalation — she's winning an argument with a trick-or-treater and she knows it. The repeated 'shut up' escalation is well-paced.

jokes.text: No, I got it. I'm good. I got it. / Wait, I had one more thing to say. Right. Shut up.
jokes.setup: Monica is trying to end the shut-up argument
jokes.punchline: She thinks she's done, then remembers she had one more 'shut up' to deliver — she can't stop even when she wants to
jokes.explanation: The 'one more thing — shut up' button is a great comedic instinct. Monica's compulsive need to have the last word overriding her attempt to de-escalate is perfectly in character.

jokes.text: You're a mean old woman. / Wait! Shut.. Don't cry! Let me get my checkbook!
jokes.setup: The child cries after Monica tells him to shut up
jokes.punchline: Monica immediately capitulates and reaches for her checkbook again — the child weaponizes tears and Monica folds completely, reverting to her earlier extreme generosity
jokes.explanation: Monica's immediate crumble at the child crying — from 'shut up' to 'let me get my checkbook' — is a satisfying reversal. The callback to writing checks adds to the running gag.

jokes.text: You don't have to do this. The strength inside you means the most. You're loyal, you're honest, and you have integrity. That's the strength I want in a man. / That means nothing to me. Come on!
jokes.setup: Monica tries to philosophize her way out of paying the crying child
jokes.punchline: The kid's flat 'That means nothing to me. Come on!' rejects Monica's moral lecture entirely — a child's mercenary honesty defeating adult philosophy
jokes.explanation: The juxtaposition of Monica's earnest moral speech and the child's brutal pragmatism is excellent. 'That means nothing to me' is a devastating response to a good-faith attempt at a life lesson. The kid is the funniest character in this sequence.

jokes.text: Hi, liar. / Hey. / He's marrying you because he thinks the things you were saying were true.
jokes.setup: Phoebe has discovered Ursula is lying to Eric about her life
jokes.punchline: 'Hi, liar.' — the casual, almost cheerful greeting undercuts what should be a serious confrontation
jokes.explanation: 'Hi, liar' is a great opener — it's how Phoebe would say it, breezy and direct. The economy is excellent.

jokes.text: Why are you taking this so seriously? It's just a marriage. / Besides, if I cheat on him, I can call it an affair.
jokes.setup: Phoebe tells Ursula she's ruining Eric's life with her lies
jokes.punchline: Ursula's casual 'it's just a marriage' and her silver lining that cheating would at least be called an 'affair' — she's already planning the exit strategy
jokes.explanation: Dark and funny. Ursula's sociopathic pragmatism is played perfectly — she's not malicious in a cartoonish way, she just has a completely alien moral framework. 'I can call it an affair' as a silver lining is a great dark comedic beat.

jokes.text: Besides, if I cheat on him, I can call it an affair.
jokes.setup: Phoebe presses Ursula about the dishonesty of her relationship.
jokes.punchline: Ursula's genuinely unhinged logic: cheating would be an 'affair,' which sounds romantic/interesting, so it's something to look forward to.
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's best jokes. The logic is genuinely twisted — Ursula sees future infidelity as a lifestyle upgrade she's already planning. 'I can call it an affair' has a breezy nonchalance that's both horrifying and hilarious. Pure character comedy at its darkest. The economy and character integration are exceptional.

jokes.text: It's a disgusting habit, and I want you to quit now! / She's helped so many people quit.
jokes.setup: Ursula is caught in another lie (or is performing something for Eric)
jokes.punchline: The context suggests Ursula has fabricated a story about helping people quit a habit — Eric's earnest confirmation reveals yet another layer of her deception
jokes.explanation: A quick beat in the Ursula-lying arc. Somewhat unclear without visual context but functional as another layer of her deception comedy.

jokes.text: She's helped so many people quit.
jokes.setup: Eric seems confused; Ursula covers by crediting Phoebe as an anti-habit helper.
jokes.punchline: Ursula attributing a virtue to Phoebe with total confidence — Phoebe who is clearly not a habit cessation specialist.
jokes.explanation: Minor laugh — the improvised lie is appropriately absurd but not particularly well-developed.

jokes.text: Wow, they're both really strong. / Or equally weak.
jokes.setup: Ross and Chandler are arm-wrestling and neither is winning
jokes.punchline: Phoebe's reframe — 'or equally weak' — deflates the apparent display of strength into an embarrassing stalemate
jokes.explanation: 'Or equally weak' is a sharp reframe delivered with perfect economy. The ambiguity of a prolonged arm-wrestle suddenly becomes comedy — they might just both be weak. Very quotable.

jokes.text: Oh, God. Chandler's making his sex face.
jokes.setup: Chandler is straining during the arm-wrestle
jokes.punchline: Monica recognizes her husband's sex face in his exertion expression — implying his sex face is indistinguishable from his 'struggling' face
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's best lines. The specificity ('his sex face'), the fact that Monica says it publicly and matter-of-factly, and the implication that his sex face is apparently identical to his effort face — all land perfectly. High quotability, strong character integration (only Monica would recognize and announce this), excellent economy. Approaches anchor-level territory.

jokes.text: Getting a little tired, though. / God, I'm exhausted.
jokes.setup: Ross and Chandler are still locked in the arm-wrestle, both claiming they could do it all day
jokes.punchline: Seconds later, both rapidly admit exhaustion — the bravado collapses almost immediately
jokes.explanation: A quick escalation-reversal. The bravado-to-exhaustion collapse is predictable but timed well.

jokes.text: This is starting to look bad for me, okay? Mona's standing right there. / She's talking to Joey! You gotta let me win!
jokes.setup: Ross is losing the arm-wrestle or stalling
jokes.punchline: Ross's reason for needing to win is that Mona is watching — but his panic intensifies when she's not watching, because now he needs Joey to sandbag instead
jokes.explanation: Ross's desperate negotiating during the arm-wrestle — asking Chandler to let him win for image reasons — is good character comedy. His reasoning is pathetically relatable.

jokes.text: Let me win. My wife thinks I'm a wimp. / At least you have a wife. I get divorces and knock people up. / And I'm dressed as doodie.
jokes.setup: Both Ross and Chandler are negotiating who deserves to win the arm-wrestle more
jokes.punchline: Ross catalogues his misfortunes: multiple divorces, an unplanned pregnancy. Then his button — 'And I'm dressed as doodie' — reduces all of his life's disasters to the costume indignity
jokes.explanation: This is the episode's comedic peak. The escalation of Ross's genuine life misfortunes — divorces, unplanned pregnancy — landing on the bathetic final humiliation of 'and I'm dressed as doodie' is a perfect comedic structure. It's dark, self-aware, character-specific, and emotionally resonant. The 'doodie' callback gives it an absurd punctuation that deflates all the pathos perfectly. This approaches the anchor-level '8' benchmark for craft.

jokes.text: Please? She's watching. / Fine. / Thanks. / Oh, no. / Oh, yeah! / My hero! / You're a weird lady.
jokes.setup: Chandler agrees to let Ross win; Mona watches
jokes.punchline: Mona's 'My hero!' is ironic (she presumably knows or suspects it was thrown); Chandler's 'You're a weird lady' is a perfect deadpan capper
jokes.explanation: The aftermath of the thrown match. 'You're a weird lady' is a funny, slightly confused response to Mona's enthusiasm. Functional button on the arm-wrestle arc.

jokes.text: I don't think I'm gonna make it to the wedding. / I wish you all the luck in the world. And I also want to give you a little piece of advice that I give to everyone who's getting married. Don't trust your wife.
jokes.setup: Chandler speaks with Eric (who is about to marry the deceptive Ursula)
jokes.punchline: Chandler's advice 'don't trust your wife' is meant as a universal warning but is accidentally perfectly targeted at Eric's specific situation
jokes.explanation: The dramatic irony — Chandler's cynical general advice is accidentally the most relevant thing Eric could hear — makes this land. The audience is ahead of Chandler, which adds a layer.

jokes.text: And I also want to give you a little piece of advice that I give to everyone who's getting married. Don't trust your wife.
jokes.setup: Phoebe gives Eric pre-wedding advice, framing it as universal wisdom.
jokes.punchline: 'Don't trust your wife' — presented as standard advice Phoebe gives to everyone, which reveals both the specific warning to Eric and the bleak worldview Phoebe carries from her experiences with Ursula.
jokes.explanation: Good dark comedy line from Phoebe. The framing 'advice I give to everyone' makes the specific warning seem like a general philosophy — which is funnier and sadder than a targeted accusation.

jokes.text: I can't let you do this. She's lying. / Okay. Yeah, not a prayer chain. / But what looks like a detailed drawing of a bank floor plan.
jokes.setup: Phoebe grabs Ursula's purse to prove she's lying — looking for evidence
jokes.punchline: The purse contains not a prayer chain but a bank floor plan — Ursula isn't just a liar, she might be planning a robbery
jokes.explanation: The bank floor plan is a great escalation of Ursula's villainy. The specificity is funny — not just 'something criminal' but a 'detailed drawing of a bank floor plan.' Ursula is revealed to be worse than a liar, potentially a would-be bank robber. Dark and funny.

jokes.text: It's so perfect, and she's been saving herself for me.
jokes.setup: Eric speaks adoringly about Ursula, sharing intimate details
jokes.punchline: The audience knows Ursula is a serial liar with a bank robbery floor plan in her purse — 'she's been saving herself' is the most ironic thing he could say
jokes.explanation: Dramatic irony — the audience understands how wrong Eric is. The joke depends entirely on what we know about Ursula, not on craft in the line itself. Functional but not particularly well-constructed.

jokes.text: Here's her name tag from where she works as a waitress. / Not a teacher, a waitress.
jokes.setup: Phoebe is exposing Ursula's lies one by one from the contents of her purse
jokes.punchline: The name tag proves she's a waitress, not a teacher — the first verifiable lie in a cascade of revelations
jokes.explanation: Functional plot beat and mild laugh. Part of the escalating exposure sequence.

jokes.text: She always lies about this. How old did she say she was? / She told me she was 25. / I almost don't want to show you. Just remember, I'm a minute younger.
jokes.setup: Phoebe prepares Eric for the truth about Ursula's age — Ursula claimed to be 25.
jokes.punchline: 'Just remember, I'm a minute younger' — implying the ID will show Ursula's real age, which Phoebe shares, and that Phoebe is at pains to distance herself from by one minute.
jokes.explanation: The 'I'm a minute younger' caveat is Phoebe-specific and sharp — she's both exposing Ursula and protecting her own ego in the same beat. Character-specific vanity with good economy.

jokes.text: She always lies about this. How old did she say she was? / She told me she was 25. / I almost don't want to show you. Just remember, I'm a minute younger.
jokes.setup: Phoebe is about to reveal Ursula's real age via ID
jokes.punchline: 'Just remember, I'm a minute younger' — Phoebe softens the blow by emphasizing she is younger than whatever age they're about to see, implying it's significantly older than 25
jokes.explanation: 'I'm a minute younger' is a beautifully constructed self-serving disclaimer. Phoebe is both helping Eric and protecting her own vanity simultaneously — the twin dynamic is perfectly used here. The audience's anticipation of how old the ID says and Phoebe's preemptive caveat make this land very well. High quotability.

jokes.text: Of course she's not a teacher. There's no such thing as a 'Top Secret School for the Children of Spies.'
jokes.setup: Eric is processing all of Ursula's lies
jokes.punchline: He reveals an even more elaborate lie he believed — Ursula told him she taught at a 'Top Secret School for the Children of Spies' — which is so absurd it's funny that he ever believed it
jokes.explanation: 'Top Secret School for the Children of Spies' is a brilliantly specific absurd invention. The joke has two layers: Ursula invented something ridiculous, and Eric believed it. The specificity is what makes it exceptional — it's not just 'spy school,' it's 'for the CHILDREN of spies,' which adds an extra layer of absurdity. One of the episode's funniest lines.

jokes.text: No, you're not stupid. / I'm not smart.
jokes.setup: Phoebe tells Eric he's not stupid for being deceived
jokes.punchline: Eric's alternative self-assessment — 'I'm not smart' — accepts Phoebe's comfort while still indicting himself
jokes.explanation: Economical and funny — the logical distinction between 'not stupid' and 'smart' is used to comedic effect. Eric accepts the comfort but demands some self-criticism. The deadpan delivery would make this land well.

jokes.text: Hurry up! I gotta pray!
jokes.setup: Ursula is leaving after being exposed as a liar who faked being religious
jokes.punchline: She shouts that she needs to 'pray' — maintaining the religious persona as she storms out, even as the deception has been exposed
jokes.explanation: A quick dark comedic button — Ursula's total shamelessness is funny. She's been exposed but still commits to the bit on her way out the door.

jokes.text: I had to give the kid 50 bucks to stop crying. / That's not bad. / I also had to go to a few houses as his girlfriend.
jokes.setup: Monica reports back on her trick-or-treat standoff resolution
jokes.punchline: Beyond paying the kid $50, Monica also had to accompany him trick-or-treating as his 'girlfriend' — a humiliating escalation that far exceeds the original problem
jokes.explanation: The reveal that Monica had to go trick-or-treating as a child's girlfriend is a perfect escalation. The build — '$50, that's not bad' — makes the second revelation land harder. This is a great comedic structure: lull the audience into thinking it's resolved, then hit with the real indignity. High impact.

jokes.text: I am awful with children. / You're good with kids. They're just crazy on Halloween. / They're all greedy, hopped up on sugar. / That's all it is? / Absolutely. Halloween is the worst. Except for Christmas. And their birthdays. / They get crazy during the summer too. / And any time they're hungry or sleepy. / Kids are tough. Good luck with that.
jokes.setup: Monica reassures Rachel (pregnant) that kids are only crazy on Halloween
jokes.punchline: Monica's reassurance progressively unravels as she lists more and more times kids are crazy — Halloween, Christmas, birthdays, summer, when hungry, when sleepy — before concluding 'Kids are tough. Good luck with that.'
jokes.explanation: Beautifully structured escalation. Monica starts comforting and ends by describing essentially the entire childhood. 'Kids are tough. Good luck with that' is a devastating button, especially aimed at a pregnant woman. The structure — reassurance that keeps collapsing — is a classic comedic build done well. High impact.

jokes.text: Look, I'm sorry you lost. / I got a secret for you. I let him win. / Was that a secret, or a lie?
jokes.setup: Chandler tells Mona he actually let Ross win the arm-wrestle
jokes.punchline: Mona's response — 'Was that a secret, or a lie?' — perfectly skewers Chandler's self-serving claim, which is unprovable and convenient
jokes.explanation: 'Was that a secret, or a lie?' is a perfectly constructed question — it acknowledges both possibilities and lets the audience decide. Economical, sharp, and character-revealing for Mona (she's perceptive). High quotability.

jokes.text: Chandler 'let me win.' / No, Chandler's really strong. My arm is so sore. Oh, nurse?
jokes.setup: Chandler asks Ross to confirm he let him win; Ross does so sarcastically and with air quotes
jokes.punchline: Ross immediately calls the nurse for his legitimately sore arm — proving the match was actually hard for him
jokes.explanation: Ross's sarcastic confirmation followed by the immediate physical evidence (sore arm, calling for the nurse) is a good double-layered joke. The 'Oh, nurse?' is a great button that proves Chandler wasn't sandbagging as much as he claims.

jokes.text: I am strong. I'll show you. / Chandler, please. / What's the matter? Scared? / Let's go, big bunny! / One, two, three. Go! / I'm gonna kill myself!
jokes.setup: Chandler, stung by the doubt about his arm-wrestle, insists on a rematch
jokes.punchline: The rematch immediately goes catastrophically — 'I'm gonna kill myself!' suggests Chandler loses even faster or suffers an injury, ending the episode on a physical comedy button
jokes.explanation: 'Let's go, big bunny!' from one of the women is a funny reminder of Chandler's humiliating costume mid-trash talk. 'I'm gonna kill myself!' as an episode ender is a solid comedic button — the hyperbolic defeat. 'Big bunny' is the best individual line here.

tmdb_overview: Monica and Chandler decide to throw a costumed Halloween party. Meanwhile, Phoebe runs into Ursula, who's preparing to get married soon, and as a courtesy invites her and her fiancé to the party. When they finally meet, Phoebe takes an instant liking to him, but soon she discovers that he knows nothing about the "real" Ursula.
insight: Halloween costumes drive character comedy harder than usual, but 77 score shows limits of pure escalation.
